articles.title: Afghan women with UK university offers 'heartbroken' after visas stopped
articles.summary: In March this year, the UK Home Office announced an "emergency visa brake" on study visas for applicants from Afghanistan.
articles.body:
When Shahira Sadat received an invitation for a Chevening Scholarship interview, she felt a rare glimmer of hope.

The software engineer in Kabul had spent three years battling Taliban restrictions, jumping through hoops and working through power and internet outages to prepare her applications for UK universities and grants.

"I was so happy. I can't describe it because I allowed myself to dream about studying in the UK," she says.

But in March this year, the UK's Home Office announced an "emergency visa brake" on study visas for applicants from Cameroon, Myanmar, Sudan and Afghanistan. Skilled work visas for Afghans were also paused. It said the move was a response to widespread visa abuse and had been triggered by a sharp rise in asylum claims from these visa routes.

At the time, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she was "taking the unprecedented decision to refuse visas for those nationals seeking to exploit our generosity". The US barred all visas for Afghan nationals earlier in the year.

Sadat had three acceptance letters to study a masters in AI and machine learning from Sussex, Bradford and Northeastern University London. Now with a shot at getting funding from the UK government-funded Chevening scheme, she felt the education she'd been denied in Afghanistan was finally within reach.

Then came an email saying she would no longer be considered to study in the UK because she was from Afghanistan.

"It was really heartbreaking. I lost all my motivation. I cried for hours and hours," says Sadat, her eyes welling up with tears. "It was not just about education for me; it was the opportunity to resume my career and to build a future for myself."

In Afghanistan, diktats from the Taliban's supreme leader have severely restricted the lives of women. They cannot attend secondary schools or universities, and are barred from most forms of work.

In the western city of Herat, Alia - whose name we have changed - received a similar rejection to Sadat. Her offers to do a digital media masters in the UK were withdrawn, which she says left her feeling trapped.

"Everything is banned just because I am an Afghan woman," she says, her voice cracking with emotion.

In a highly competitive field of international students vying to get UK scholarships, Afghan women have additional challenges to navigate.

Alia had to attend a secret school to prepare for an English language test, in defiance of Taliban restrictions. Before long the institute was discovered and authorities shut it down - so she continued with an online teacher from Canada.

The next challenge was actually sitting the test. Most authorised test centres would not admit female students, Sadat says, in fear of falling foul of the regime's rules.

After that came the difficulty of finding a UK university willing to recognise a degree earned in Afghanistan.

Throughout the process, both Sadat and Alia say frequent power cuts disrupted their preparations. They also feared a repeat of the nationwide internet shutdown imposed by the Taliban's supreme leader in September 2025.

Many students also find it difficult to physically apply for the visas, as they often have to travel to neighbouring countries which are making it harder for Afghan nationals to enter.

Having overcome the obstacles, Alia finds the visa brake deeply disappointing: "I want to say to the UK government: don't treat us like our government. They have deprived us of education, so the global community should have more focus on us."

In response to the BBC's questions about the suspensions, the UK's Home Office pointed to the reopening of the UK Resettlement Scheme for refugees, "including Afghan women and girls". It also said it was introducing "named sponsorship and refugee study routes", which would give refugees "a safe pathway to come to the UK and rebuild their lives".

However, the Home Office did not answer specific questions about whether these routes would be open to women in Afghanistan who are not classified as refugees, such as Sadat and Alia, or how many places would be available to Afghans.

Data from the Higher Education Statistics Agency shows that fewer than 400 of the more than 680,000 international students in the UK in 2024-25 were from Afghanistan.

Since this article was published, the Home Office has contacted the BBC to share data which shows that in the three years before the visa brake was applied the number of asylum claims from Afghans linked to study visa routes have outstripped the number of visas issued. From January to September 2025, there were 360 study visas issued and 470 asylum claims linked to these visas, while in 2024, 550 asylum claims came from 470 study visas that were issued.

We asked Zainab Rezaie, an Afghan student who moved to Birmingham in 2024 and later applied for asylum, why she made that choice.

Rezaie, who is pursuing a PhD in education at the University of Exeter, says she was "very anxious" about what would happen after she graduated. She feared that if her visa expired before she could secure a job or switch to another visa, she would have no choice but to return to Taliban-run Afghanistan where - especially given her field of studies - she would not be able to work, and the possibilities of her life would be severely limited.

Rezaie says she applied for asylum to "give myself some opportunity to think".

"The biggest contrast is that I'm not in prison in my room. I have the right to move around every day, to go out, to exercise, to buy something. Living in Western society, you may never think that the freedom to go out at any time is a big advantage. But in Afghanistan, every move women make has to be strategised."

She says it was "never my choice" to come and live in the UK as an asylum seeker. "It takes a lot of mental effort to live here on your own and to be separated from your family, to adjust to society… Nobody chooses this happily, willingly."

There are still opportunities for Afghans to study abroad, in Europe, Asia and elsewhere, but the women we spoke to fear other countries will follow in the US and UK's footsteps.

They feel the international community is slowly closing its doors on them.

articles.title: Tube Girl: Sabrina Bahsoon on being 'written off' as psychotic
articles.summary: The content creator's self-shot videos of her dancing on the London Underground blew up online in 2023.
articles.body:
Sabrina Bahsoon became known globally as Tube Girl after self-shot videos of her dancing and lip-syncing on the London Underground blew up online.

The 26-year-old content creator had the world at her feet when she went viral in 2023 , going on to build a social media following of more than 900,000 people.

She signed major brand endorsement deals and was pursuing a music career.

But then her "whole life turned upside down" when she had what appeared to be a psychotic episode.

Her symptoms made her violent and erratic, leading to her being sectioned in a mental health hospital - where doctors treated her with anti-psychotic medication.

But Bahsoon's family, helped by her father's neurologist friend, pushed for further tests.

And two months into her hospital treatment, doctors got to the truth.

She actually had a rare, but treatable, autoimmune disease which is known to sometimes present as psychiatric symptoms, as well as seizures, confusion and memory loss.

In her first interview since the experience, she tells BBC News she wants hospitals to offer a series of tests as standard practice if patients have these symptoms.

"In a way I do feel let down by the care I received. I feel like the urgency to discover what was actually wrong with me wasn't there," she says.

"And I also feel as a woman being written off completely as a psychotic patient without further investigation was a mistake."

A spokesperson for the hospital she attended has apologised for Bahsoon's experience and says an investigation has been launched into her care.

Bahsoon first had "psychotic symptoms" in March this year after filming a video on the Tube with girl group Flo.

She says that evening she began to scream, cry and her conversations became "very erratic".

The next day she broke up with her boyfriend, which prompted her sisters to check on her, as it was so unexpected.

Bahsoon says her condition got worse, becoming violent towards herself and posting videos which didn't make sense, before her sisters called 999 for an ambulance.

"I'm normally a very relaxed person, maybe anxious at times, but the way I was speaking about harming myself and the way I was screaming and being violent was super out of character for me," she says.

A&E doctors initially thought her symptoms could have been provoked by stress and a lack of sleep, discharging her with sleeping tablets.

She then began destroying things at home and spoke about having hallucinations, which led to police bringing her to hospital in handcuffs.

Bahsoon was sectioned and moved to a psychiatric ward where she was treated with antipsychotic medication, which she says made her "docile".

"I went from being a total firecracker to being completely catatonic," she says.

"I stopped eating, drinking. I could not speak properly."

Bahsoon has "very faint memories" of this period, she says, but her family has since shown her clips of her having breakdowns which she finds "heartbreaking".

After two months on the psychiatric ward, Bahsoon was diagnosed with an autoimmune disease called anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

It was caused by tumours in her ovaries, known as teratomas, producing antibodies which attacked her body.

She had surgery to remove the tumours in June, which she says brought on a "drastic" change in her behaviour from "freaking out" to having more understanding of what was happening around her.

Bahsoon has since been recovering back in her home country of Malaysia and is having therapy to "deal with all the trauma".

But she says she feels "very lucky" as doctors have told her she is part of a small percentage of people who they expect to make a full recovery.

The content creator first revealed what happened in a TikTok video in October, and says she is sharing her story as she wants to raise awareness of the disease.

She also wants to "push people to advocate for themselves" if they feel they're not getting the "treatment they deserve".

"I do want reform in the way that hospitals deal with psychotic patients or patients that present with psychotic symptoms," she says.

"I hope I'm sharing my story so that nobody else has to go through this."

She plans to return to her content creation in the new year and is looking forward to "enjoying life with a whole new perspective and appreciation for what I do and what I now can help people with".

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is more typical in women and mainly affects young people, with about 40% of cases aged under 18, according to the charity Encephalitis International (EI) .

Dr Ava Easton MBE, chief executive of EI, says a "frightening" aspect is how quickly someone's behaviour and personality can appear to change.

"A person may suddenly seem confused, distressed or [to be] experiencing psychosis when the underlying problem is actually inflammation of their brain," she says.

She says there's a "real risk" of it going undiagnosed and encourages people to look out for the warning signs .

According to the NHS , cases of all types of encephalitis are rare, and EI says the condition affects about 6,000 people in the UK each year.

A spokesperson for Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust, which was the first to treat Bahsoon, said they were "very sorry" for what she experienced.

They said an internal review found some aspects of her initial assessment "were not followed up as they should have been" and an investigation had been started.

Dr Ed Beveridge, divisional medical director at Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust, also confirmed they'd be part of that review.

He said anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis was a "rare autoimmune condition" that is not "routinely screened for nationally".

"We are pleased that her condition has now been identified and treated."

If you have been affected by the issues raised in this article, help and support is available via BBC Action Line .

articles.title: State failing to keep public safe, warns victims' commissioner
articles.summary: Claire Waxman tells the BBC Andy Burnham needs to put justice in his 10-year plan for government.
articles.body:
The victims' commissioner for England and Wales has said the state is failing to keep the public safe, as she urged Andy Burnham to put the justice system at the heart of his 10-year plan for government.

Claire Waxman told the BBC that she would press the prime minister to commit to reforms in the decade-long blueprint, which he is set to unveil next month.

She warned that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding in jails, along with long waits in the courts, had eroded the trust of crime victims to come forward.

It comes as the commissioner's latest annual survey of victims, to be published on Tuesday, found many had experienced long waits for justice.

Nearly half of respondents whose case went to a crown court had seen their trial postponed, with over a quarter reporting the trial had taken place more than a year after it was originally scheduled.

Almost half of the respondents to the survey also said they were dissatisfied with communication from the police.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Waxman said the results showed victims were being failed "at every point".

The commissioner, who said she was due to meet Burnham in the coming weeks, said she wanted him to put a "real commitment to reforming our criminal justice system" as part of his 10-year plan.

"It's been under-invested and mismanaged for so many years. That's why we're in the state that we're in," she added.

She warned: "It can't continue. Otherwise I will be in a position as the victims' commissioner to have to be very honest and open with victims publicly to say there's no point coming forward and reporting."

Asked whether the state was failing in its duty to keep the public safe, she replied: "It is failing", adding that the early release of prisoners could lead to the potentially risky offenders being supervised by a probation service "on its knees".

Waxman also criticised the government's handling of the scheme, saying that victims needed further reassurance that they would be kept safe when offenders are let out under the programme to ease overcrowding in jails.

Around 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to eventually be released under the latest version of the scheme , the need for which Labour has blamed on a lack of investment in prisons under the Conservatives.

Waxman said that letters sent over the summer to warn victims ahead of releases had been "very poor" and lacked detail on how offenders were going to be risk-assessed prior to being let out early.

She said she was "still waiting to see" data about the impact of releases on the ground, adding it had been around a year since the last meeting of the National Criminal Justice Board, an oversight body for the justice system.

As part of the latest survey, the commissioner is recommending that all crime victims should receive a victim identifier number to track their progress through the criminal justice system.

The survey report will argue this would improve coordination between different agencies, as well as allowing victims to monitor when they will access the various legal rights they have under the Victims' Code.

It will also call for an "end-to-end" review of how victims navigate the system, similar to recent reviews that have focused on sentencing or the courts.

Responding to the survey results, Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones said the government was doing "everything we can to fix the broken system we inherited".

She added that ministers had already taken steps to improve the court backlog, and would be publishing an update to the Victims' Code next year.

She said this would be easier for victims to understand, and would set "clear expectations for criminal justice agencies and help victims feel supported".

articles.title: Rare goats drafted in to tame steep Greenwich Park hillside
articles.summary: Bagot goats are used to keep vegetation in check and help preserve the view from the Royal Observatory.
articles.body:
A park in south-east London has taken on some new groundskeepers, and they are more than happy to eat on the job.

A small herd of rare Bagot goats has been brought in to clear a steep, overgrown slope below the Royal Observatory in Greenwich Park, in a trial run by The Royal Parks charity.

Over five days the animals will chomp through tough, woody plants and thorny stems on Castle Hill Bank, a patch that is hard to reach with machinery or by hand.

Visitors can watch them at work until Friday, between 11:00 and 15:30 GMT.

The trial uses conservation grazing, a traditional method in which animals keep dominant vegetation in check, giving other plants room to grow and supporting wildlife.

The Royal Parks is working with Mudchute Park and Farm, on the Isle of Dogs, and the Rare Breeds Survival Trust, with funding from players of People's Postcode Lottery.

Bagots are Britain's oldest native breed of goat, according to the charity. They are small and light-footed, which makes them well suited to steep and uneven ground.

Clare Lanes, Greenwich Park manager, said the view of Flamsteed House above the bank was part of what made the park so special as a Unesco World Heritage Site.

"But it's a very steep bank, and managing vegetation to protect that view is a real challenge," she said.

"We're trialling a traditional approach by bringing in goats to graze, which we hope will help us protect the landscape more sustainably."

She said the approach could also help the charity in its ambition to create climate-resilient parks for future generations as well as making a few visitors smile.

The herd is kept in a paddock with a lean-to shelter and fresh water, and is shepherded on and off site each day.

The goats are being watched over by Tom Davis, farm manager at Mudchute, which has previously worked with The Royal Parks on similar projects in other London parks.

He said the scheme was giving an "incredibly rare breed" an important purpose.

Charlotte Cass, who manages The Royal Parks' Help Nature Thrive project, said the charity was "always looking for exciting ways to support nature" and new ways to manage its eight London parks.

"This project helps create a better, more viable habitat for invertebrates, birds and small mammals in Greenwich Park in the longer term," she said.

articles.title: Village featured in Hollywood films could get new parking scheme amid influx of tourists
articles.summary: Locals say illegal parking by visitors creates an 'unpleasant' situation.
articles.body:
A residents' parking scheme could be introduced in a Cotswold village popular with visitors.

Castle Combe in Wiltshire, previously named one of the "prettiest villages in England", can be packed with tourists, especially at the weekends and on bank holidays.

Famous for being the backdrop to films like Stardust and War Horse, people flock to the village's bridge over the River Bybrook which offers a stunning backdrop to photos.

But people who call Castle Combe home say the parking situation can become "unpleasant" when visitors block driveways or park illegally, which makes already narrow roads harder to navigate.

Lorry driver arrested after pedestrian dies in collision

"Castle Combe has been a tourist destination for more than 100 years," explained John Mackelden, chairman of the local parish council. "It's an unspoiled village, so it's always a draw [to people].

"But the car park fills up quite quickly, which leads to challenges elsewhere. When people decide to go here for their Sunday afternoon walk, they can be very tenacious.

"If the car park is full, they don't think about going somewhere else - they think 'I have decided to come to Castle Combe today, even if that does mean leaving my car in someone's hedge'."

The parish council is working with Wiltshire Council to develop plans for a residents' parking scheme which will span the entire village centre.

Martin Smith, cabinet member for highways and transport, said: "The proposed scheme aims to help manage parking demand, improve access for residents, and support the safe and efficient operation of the highway network, while recognising Castle Combe's popularity as a visitor destination."

"Residents would have to pay," explained Mackelden. "But they are quite happy to do that because the situation is pretty bad."

He said locals have had their driveways blocked by cars and that illegal parking recently delayed a fire engine by 20 minutes as it could not get down one stretch of road as cars were parked either side.

Visitors also sometimes park on a steep hill that leads down from the public car park or on yellow lines in the centre of the village.

"I think most residents would agree over the last couple of years in particularly, the situation has got so that it can be really quite unpleasant living in the village sometimes," Mackelden added.

"We're doing our best to resolve the issues we've got."

The scheme will progress through a Traffic Regulation Order process between Thursday and 21 December when people will be able to give feedback on it.

If approved, the permit scheme would come into force fully during 2027.

Similar schemes are in the works for Bourton-on-the-Water in Gloucestershire and in Weston-super-Mare in Somerset.

articles.title: In 2025, a Washington couple bought a $156,000 lot, built their 1,400-square-foot home in nine months on a $209,000 budget and now pay under $900 a month
articles.summary: Discover how a Washington couple turned their homeownership dream into reality by building their own house on a budget, keeping their monthly payments under $900.
articles.body: Buying a home might feel like a distant dream for many young people. But one couple in Washington state found another way to turn that dream into a reality. Maddy Olson, 27, and her husband Drew built their own house to keep their mortgage payment low, Business Insider reports. The couple built the home in about nine months, and now their payment is less than $900 a month.A dream that began with rentingThe Olsons tied the knot in 2019 and were renting at the time, but they already had dreams about owning a place. At some point, the Olsons’ landlord even offered to sell them the property for $249,000. That price was out of reach for them at the time, so they decided to focus on saving money while building up their careers. Maddy is a content creator and owns the drink brand Over Ice Soda, while Drew works in commercial concrete. The couple bought the lot for $156,000 in January 2025. It turned out to be smaller than expected, but it was near a cousin's home. Maddy also liked that the small plot made it almost impossible to overspend. A set budget and a lot of hands-on workThe couple set a building budget of $209,000 and got a construction loan. Their main savings came from hands-on labour. Drew had some construction experience, though it was his first time doing most of the work. The HVAC system and drywall were done by professionals, but the pair did almost everything else by themselves. They began building in September 2025, lived in a rental for the majority of the build and stayed with Drew's parents near the end. Maddy’s mother and mother-in-law looked after her daughter. The home is built on an existing 1,400-square-foot builder's plan with three bedrooms, two and a half bathrooms and some minor changes. They moved in at the end of May 2026.Bargains, splurges and mistakesAlthough Maddy had no tiling experience, she tiled both bathrooms. She looked for good deals from Habitat for Humanity ReStore and Facebook Marketplace. She also bought her daughter's bathroom vanity from Marketplace and even had a professional paint it for her. Kitchen cabinets came in pieces and were assembled at home, which saved money; then $5,700 went to a marble island. Mistakes were also made in the process. They didn't realise that the outlet locations had to be settled before the drywall went up. After the frame was up, the house appeared darker than they wanted. So Drew added some more windows. He also later rebuilt the staircase to suit Maddy’s design wishes.Design choices and life on site Maddy led the design and wanted it to feel like a warm California cottage. Some people in the Pacific Northwest favour deep greens, but she gets low in winter, so she chose warm neutrals. Her daughter's bathroom floor was done in a floral penny-tile pattern, and the walls were painted butter-yellow to match. Lighting came from Amazon, and flooring was from Floor & Decor. Her mum, who is building a tiny home, will take over the leftover bathroom tile. Drew works at his parents' company, so he was able to build on slower days. Maddy documented the process on TikTok, including moments showing her removing tile from a wall and repainting it twice after she disliked the colour. She also told Business Insider that she retiled rooms repeatedly. By her own account, she wanted to cry every day, but it was worth it in the end.What comes next for the OlsonsThe house is mostly done. Their daughter's room and the third bedroom are yet to be decorated. However, they managed to work within budget, and Maddy calls a payment of less than $900 a month amazing for her family. They plan to live there for a few years. Then they hope to buy land, build a bigger house and rent this one out. This route takes time, effort and family support, and it may not work for everyone. articles.title: In 1969, film critic Rex Reed bought an apartment in New York’s famous Dakota building for just $30,000; after nearly 60 years, the two-bedroom home is listed for $5.99 million to support his foundation
articles.summary: A Manhattan apartment that witnessed nearly six decades of Hollywood history is now on the property market, carrying an asking price of $5.99 million.
articles.body: A Manhattan apartment that witnessed nearly six decades of Hollywood history is now on the property market, carrying an asking price of $5.99 million. The former home of late film critic and journalist Rex Reed, located inside New York City’s celebrated Dakota building, is being offered for $5,999,000, with proceeds from the sale and an accompanying estate auction set to support the Rex Reed Foundation. Realtor dot com first reported the listing, while 6sqft and Robb Report have also highlighted the property’s connection to the veteran film critic. Reed purchased the two-bedroom apartment in 1969 for $30,000 and remained there until his death on May 12, 2026, at the age of 87. According to the Associated Press, he spent more than six decades as a prominent voice in American film and cultural criticism, writing for publications including The New York Times, Vogue, Esquire and The New York Observer.The apartment, identified as Residence 86, occupies a high floor of the Dakota at 1 West 72nd Street on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. Spanning approximately 2,000 square feet, the two-bedroom, two-bathroom residence retains its original pre-war layout, with a formal entrance gallery, a large living room and a separate dining room. The property was listed on November 13 through Sotheby’s International Realty.Its interiors reflect the character of a home accumulated over decades rather than a recently designed luxury residence. The apartment features high ceilings, oak flooring, Regency-style doors and crown mouldings, alongside north- and west-facing windows that offer views across the surrounding cityscape. The formal dining room also includes a pantry and dry bar, while both bedrooms have en-suite bathrooms and generous closet space.Reed used the second bedroom as his office, where built-in shelves accommodated his extensive collection of books and films. The apartment also served as a gathering place for personalities from the entertainment world. Over the years, Reed hosted guests including Lauren Bacall, Boris Karloff and Truman Capote, making the residence part of New York’s wider cultural history.The building itself adds considerably to the property’s appeal. Completed in 1884 and designed by architect Henry J. Hardenbergh, who also designed the Plaza Hotel, the Dakota is regarded as one of Manhattan’s most recognisable residential landmarks. Its distinctive architecture, featuring elaborate gables, arches and ornate detailing, has made it a fixture of Central Park West. The building also gained wider recognition through its association with notable residents, including John Lennon.According to the property listing, the Dakota offers residents a gated entrance, a landscaped central courtyard with restored fountains, concierge services, a resident manager and a fitness centre. Monthly maintenance for the apartment is listed at $8,842. The building permits pets and pieds-à-terre, while buyers can finance up to 50 per cent of the purchase price.The sale is also accompanied by an auction of Reed’s personal collection. Auction house Doyle organised a November 23 sale featuring furniture, artwork, books, decorations and memorabilia from his Dakota residence, offering collectors an opportunity to acquire pieces associated with the critic’s private life.The proceeds from the apartment sale and the estate auction are intended to benefit the Rex Reed Foundation, established to honour his legacy and support storytelling and cultural initiatives. The foundation’s website describes its mission as recognising Reed’s contribution to American cultural criticism and preserving his influence across film, theatre, literature and entertainment. The listing marks the end of a remarkable chapter for an apartment that remained Reed’s home through changing eras of New York life. What began as a $30,000 purchase in 1969 is now a nearly $6 million property, with its next sale expected to carry forward the legacy of the man who called it home for almost six decades.You use AI every day. articles.title: Barnet footballer Isiah Noel-Williams charged with rape
articles.summary: Isiah Noel-Williams, from St Albans, is remanded in custody charged with three rape offences.
articles.body:
League Two footballer Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged with rape.

Noel-Williams, who plays for League Two side Barnet, has been charged with three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault by penetration, Hertfordshire Police said.

The 23-year-old, of High Oaks, St Albans, was remanded in custody following a hearing at Hatfield Magistrates' Court on Saturday.

In a statement, the club said it was "co-operating fully with authorities" and would determine further action "in due course".

Noel-Williams has also been charged with one count of engaging in sexual communication with a child, and one count of supplying a controlled (Class B) drug, police added.

In a statement, the London club said: "Barnet FC can confirm that first-team player Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged and remanded in custody as part of a police investigation by Hertfordshire Constabulary.

"The club is co-operating fully with the authorities and will determine any further action in due course.

"As this is now a matter for the courts, the club will not be making any further comment."

Noel-Williams, who previously played for Hemel Hempstead Town, Kettering Town, Matlock Town, Harrow Borough and Cheshunt, joined Barnet in June.

articles.title: Snowflake billionaire Frank Slootman and wife Brenda give $1,000 each to 22,081 Montana children who missed Trump's federal seed money; the donation will give them an early financial head start through tax-advantaged investment accounts
articles.summary: Billionaire technology executive Frank Slootman and his wife Brenda have committed $22.081 million to provide $1,000 each to 22,081 children across
articles.body: Billionaire technology executive Frank Slootman and his wife Brenda have committed $22.081 million to provide $1,000 each to 22,081 children across Montana through the Trump Accounts programme. The donation targets children born in 2023 and 2024, who fall outside the birth-year eligibility window for the US government's separate $1,000 seed contribution. Announced by the US Department of the Treasury on November 19, 2026, the contribution is being made through the Slootman Family Foundation. According to the foundation, the money has already been deposited and invested in the children's accounts. The initiative aims to give these children an early financial asset that can potentially grow through long-term investments before they reach adulthood.Why are these children receiving $1,000 from the billionaire couple?The donation is aimed at a specific group of children who do not qualify for the federal government's initial $1,000 contribution under the Trump Accounts programme.Under the federal scheme, eligible US citizen children born between January 1, 2025, and December 31, 2028, with valid Social Security numbers can receive a one-time $1,000 contribution from the US Treasury Department. However, parents or guardians must submit the required election to claim this contribution, even if an account has already been opened automatically.Children born in 2023 and 2024 fall outside this particular federal seed-money window. However, they are not excluded from holding Trump Accounts. Eligible children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers can have accounts even if they do not qualify for the government's initial contribution.The Slootman Family Foundation has stepped in to provide the same $1,000 starting contribution to 22,081 children born during those two years in Montana. The total commitment amounts to $22,081,000.According to the foundation's announcement, the contributions have already been deposited through the Treasury Department and invested in the children's accounts.How will the $1,000 contributions work?The money is being deposited into Trump Accounts, which are tax-advantaged investment accounts created for eligible American children under the Working Families Tax Cuts legislation signed into law in 2025.Unlike ordinary savings accounts, these accounts are designed to hold investments that can potentially grow over an extended period. During childhood, funds are generally invested in eligible low-cost mutual funds or exchange-traded funds tracking broad US stock-market indices.Parents or guardians must claim and activate their children's accounts before they can manage them. Once an account is claimed, family members and friends can contribute towards the investment, subject to an annual combined limit of $5,000 for ordinary individual and employer contributions.Employers can contribute up to $2,500 annually towards an employee's Trump Account or that of an eligible dependent. However, this amount counts towards the same $5,000 annual limit rather than being an additional allowance. Certain government and charitable contributions are governed by separate rules and may fall outside this limit.The money is intended to remain invested for the long term. When the beneficiary reaches adulthood, the account generally becomes subject to traditional individual retirement account rules, including applicable tax and withdrawal restrictions.The accounts are not restricted to college expenses, unlike conventional education savings plans. Instead, they are designed to provide children with a financial asset that can continue growing beyond their school years.Who are Frank and Brenda Slootman?Frank Slootman is a Dutch-born American technology executive and billionaire investor known for leading several major software companies.He previously served as chief executive of Data Domain, where he led the company through its public listing in 2007 before its acquisition by EMC in 2009. He subsequently became president and CEO of ServiceNow in 2011, overseeing its growth and 2012 stock market listing.In 2019, Slootman joined cloud-data company Snowflake as its CEO and led it through its September 2020 public listing. He stepped down from the chief executive position in February 2024 but continued as chairman of the company's board. Snowflake's current CEO is Sridhar Ramaswamy.Forbes estimated his net worth at approximately $3.5 billion in November 2026. His wealth has largely been built through his leadership roles in the technology and enterprise software industries.His wife Brenda is also named as a donor in the Treasury Department's announcement. The couple are based in Bozeman, Montana, and are making the contribution through their Slootman Family Foundation.Other billionaires are also funding Trump AccountsThe Slootmans are among several wealthy individuals and families contributing to the Trump Accounts programme through private donations.Michael and Susan Dell previously pledged $6.25 billion to provide $250 contributions to approximately 25 million eligible American children born before 2025. Their initiative focuses on children aged 10 and younger living in qualifying ZIP codes with median household incomes below $150,000.According to the Slootman Family Foundation's announcement, another 118,523 Montana children qualify for the Dell family's $250 contribution, subject to the initiative's eligibility requirements.This means some children born in 2023 and 2024 could potentially benefit from both initiatives, receiving the Slootmans' $1,000 contribution as well as the separate $250 Dell contribution if they meet the relevant conditions.Investor Ray Dalio and his wife Barbara have also pledged $75 million to support contributions for eligible children in Connecticut, particularly those from lower-income households.These contributions are separate from the federal government's own $1,000 seed-money initiative. They demonstrate how private donors can use the account system to extend investment opportunities to children who may not qualify for the initial government contribution.What the donation means for Montana familiesThe contribution provides thousands of Montana families with an opportunity to begin building investment savings for their children from an early age.The Slootman Family Foundation's commitment covers 22,081 children born in 2023 and 2024 across the state, providing each with an initial $1,000 investment contribution.Montana Governor Greg Gianforte welcomed the donation, thanking the Slootman family for supporting investment accounts for children across the state. He also encouraged families to activate their children's accounts and explore the investment opportunities available through the federal programme.The foundation has encouraged parents and relatives to consider making additional contributions on birthdays, holidays and other occasions.For the children covered by the donation, the $1,000 contribution provides an investment starting point that could remain invested for many years before they reach adulthood. The eventual value will depend on investment performance and applicable account rules.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2023, conservationists laid 750 tonnes of gravel and recycled scallop shells on the northeast coast to rebuild oyster habitat; two years later, monitoring found oysters surviving and establishing despite storms shifting some reef material
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking project, 750 tonnes of gravel and scallop shells were laid to restore native oyster habitats off the northeast coast of England, with surviving oysters spotted after a severe storm, showcasing resilience in marine restoration efforts.
articles.body: Conservationists placed more than 750 tonnes of gravel and weathered scallop shells on the seabed off the coast of northeast England in September 2023. This placement created an artificial reef that was intended to help restore a marine habitat that had largely disappeared from the region. The 7,500-square-metre site was designed to provide a surface that was suitable for European native oysters to settle and grow. At the centre, the team introduced around 10,000 mature oysters, which were sourced from Scottish populations. This development formed part of the Wild Oysters Project: Tyne & Wear, a restoration initiative led by the Zoological Society of London (ZSL) and Groundwork North East and Cumbria.The material spread across the seabed is known as cultch and provides a hard surface on which young oysters can attach. This process helps to create the foundation of a reef. The 2023 development combined limestone gravel with weathered scallop shells, hence creating a condition which was suitable for oyster settlement by repurposing the shell.Why conservationists wanted to bring native oysters backEuropean native oysters were once widespread in British coastal waters. However, they noted a drastic decline in populations because of historic overharvesting, pollution, disease and the destruction of suitable seabed habitat. According to Groundwork, the native oyster population has fallen by around 95% across Europe since the 1800s. In Tyne & Wear, the species had been considered extinct for decades, prompting active restoration as a necessity.This loss is concerning because oysters do a lot more than just live on the seabeds. They are filter feeders, removing suspended particles and organic matter from surrounding water. As generations of oysters grow on top of one another, their shells form complex three-dimensional reefs. These structures are treated as shelters, feeding grounds and nursery habitats for other marine species.In addition, the project tested whether a restoration method used in more sheltered waters could work under tougher coastal conditions as experienced in an exposed North Sea location. In October 2023, Storm Babet struck the region, generating waves reported to have reached seven to eight metres. Some of the cultch and oysters were displaced from the original reef site because of the force of the storm. Later one, remotely operated vehicle surveys could not confidently establish where most of the displaced material had settled.Divers looked for oysters after the stormIn June 2024, Project Baseline UK joined Groundwork North East and Cumbria to investigate the seabed and analyse what remained. The crew used drop-camera surveys and data about the prevailing wind direction during the storm to identify the six sites for divers to explore. At each site, divers surveyed an area that extended up to 50 metres from a central point, recording where they found cultch or oysters. In addition, a small number of live oysters were brought to the surface for examination by a marine ecologist, and then the team returned those oysters to the sea.Of the 11 oysters found in the search, only five remained alive. Those surviving specimens appeared to be in decent condition. Though the quantity varied, the divers found cultch at all six survey locations. It provided a baseline for the remaining material and oyster presence, despite the survey not providing a concrete count of how many of the original 10,000 oysters had survived.The subsequent observations from Groundwork gave an insight into a broader indication of progress. Despite the storm moving some of the reef material, ongoing monitoring had found oysters surviving and establishing in the area. This could be counted as a sign that parts of the restoration effort had persisted beyond the initial disturbance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Urgent action needed to protect Buttermere, new reports warns
articles.summary: Tourism and outdated septic tanks are said to be adding to the ecological decline of Buttermere.
articles.body:
Tourism, infrastructure challenges and "outdated, undersized and poorly maintained" wastewater systems are contributing to the ecological decline of a popular lake, an environmental group has warned.

Buttermere, in the Lake District, has seen rising nutrient levels in recent years which can lead to excess phosphorus and blankets of algae.

A new report has found farming practices alone "cannot account" for the changes.

West Cumbria Rivers Trust (WCRT), a charity which tracked down the sources of phosphorus for the study, argues "urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed".

The Buttermere Nutrient Investigations Project was commissioned and funded by the Environment Agency (EA) after the lake was last year found to be failing to meet total phosphorus targets.

WCRT said the investigation showed Buttermere - a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest and Special Area of Conservation - was a "fragile ecosystem under pressure".

Buttermere is a naturally nutrient-poor lake, the organisation said, which provides a welcoming environment for sensitive species, such as the Arctic charr cold-water fish.

But algae triggered by excess phosphorus can "choke out these rare habitats and degrade the lake's protected status", WCRT added.

Local wastewater infrastructure was identified as a "key area of concern", the organisation said, while agricultural investigations across major landholdings found no evidence of systemic diffuse pollution or excessive nutrient use, with soil management plans broadly appropriate.

As they are not connected to mains drainage, many properties in the area rely on septic tanks or package treatment plants.

However, WCRT said a number of the 11 septic tank systems identified in the catchment were "undersized, poorly maintained or past their effective lifespan, with several suspected to be discharging directly to surface water, which is not compliant with the regulations".

Although most owners were keen to help the environment, the trust said there was a "widespread lack of awareness" about how the private systems worked and what level of maintenance was needed.

Surveys also revealed just over 40% of visitors had dogs with them and many were walked along sensitive lakeshore paths.

Nutrient fertilisation by the animals "could be significant", it was found.

WCRT CEO Jodie Mills, said: "Our investigations show that water quality in Buttermere is suffering primarily due to private wastewater systems that are undersized, poorly maintained or overwhelmed during peak seasonal surges.

"Many home and business owners simply didn't realise their tanks weren't performing properly.

"This creates a hidden source of pollution, and urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed to protect this special lake."

In addition to calling for regulation and enforcement, the trust said it would be providing wastewater guidance for homeowners on its website and engaging with the local parish council and the Lake District Visitor Management Group, which includes the National Trust and the Lake District National Park Authority.

Responsibility for the regulation of discharges belongs to the EA.

Peter Miles, the organisation's nature, monitoring and technical manager, said the report provided "valuable information about the sources of excess nutrients" in Buttermere.

He added: "Sources of pollution are often very complex and we urge everyone living or working in Buttermere, and those visiting, to play their part in reducing the amount of pollution entering the lake, from checking their private sewage systems to clearing up after their dogs."

articles.title: US delays 60 Patriot missiles for Ukraine as Russia intensifies attacks
articles.summary: Ukraine will have to wait longer for its desperately needed Patriot missile supplies.
articles.body: Ukraine will have to wait longer for its desperately needed Patriot missile supplies. The Pentagon has held up approval for around 60 interceptors already allocated to Kyiv, despite its western allies having paid for them.The delay comes as Russia intensifies missile attacks on Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure ahead of winter, raising fresh concerns over Kyiv's ability to defend against incoming ballistic missiles.According to a report by the Financial Times, citing two Ukrainian officials and another person familiar with the matter, the delayed allocation includes 40 advanced PAC-3 interceptors and around 20 older PAC-2 missiles. The deliveries are awaiting approval from US defence secretary Pete Hegseth.The report said the 40 PAC-3 interceptors were scheduled to arrive in four shipments between September and December. However, none of these deliveries has yet been authorised. Around 20 PAC-2 interceptors allocated to Ukraine are also awaiting approval.The two types of interceptors serve different roles in Ukraine's air defence. The advanced PAC-3 missiles use hit-to-kill technology, destroying incoming ballistic missiles through direct impact and are particularly important for countering Russia's ballistic missile attacks.The older PAC-2 interceptors, meanwhile, use a fragmentation warhead that detonates near the target, releasing shrapnel to destroy it. Both are part of the Patriot system, but PAC-3 provides Ukraine with its most critical capability against ballistic missile threats.Since the missiles are designed and manufactured in the US, Washington must authorise their export or re-export, including transfers from European stockpiles.The delay comes at a critical time for Ukraine, which is struggling to maintain supplies of interceptors amid intensifying Russian missile attacks.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Kyiv receives an average of just 12 Patriot interceptors from the US every month, while Russia launches around 150 ballistic missiles during the same period.Zelenskyy had requested a winter package of 300 Patriot interceptors from US President Donald Trump. However, Trump declined the request, citing low global stocks of the missiles. The outstanding 60 interceptors could provide some relief to Ukraine's air defence network, but their delivery remains uncertain.The Ukrainian president has repeatedly pressed Washington to approve the pending deliveries. On Sunday, Zelenskyy said it was important for the US to authorise the transfer of Patriot missiles that Kyiv's western partners had already paid for.In his Monday night address, he warned that Ukrainian intelligence had indicated Russia was preparing fresh strikes. He urged the US and other countries supplying anti-ballistic missile interceptors to pay attention to the warnings, stressing the need to protect Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.The shortage of Patriot interceptors has become a major concern as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure ahead of winter. According to the FT, Ukrainian officials warned that when Patriot launchers run out of missiles, nearly every Russian ballistic missile strikes its target inside Ukraine.The threat was underscored by a recent Russian ballistic missile attack on Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy's hometown, which killed a seven-year-old boy and a medical worker and injured 58 people. The attack highlighted the risks facing Ukrainian cities as Kyiv struggles to replenish its air defence supplies.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: A Don Toliver concert in Manchester was evacuated after an unknown substance was released into the crowd, leaving dozens of people with eye and respiratory symptoms, as police continue to investigate the incident.Greater Manchester Police said around 12,000 people were safely escorted out of Co-op Live arena after the incident during the US rapper’s performance on Sunday night. The ambulance service said several crews attended, including the Hazardous Area Response Team, and that dry decontamination was carried out as a precaution.The nature of the substance remains under investigation. While initial reports suggested tear gas may have been released, TMZ, citing sources with direct knowledge of the incident, reported that the episode was an isolated altercation in which one concertgoer allegedly used pepper spray on another.The report said the substance was not tear gas and that there had been no widespread attack on the audience. However, police have not publicly confirmed that account and said testing was continuing on items recovered from the venue.Greater Manchester Police said detectives were working to establish what the substance was, where it came from and whether any criminality had occurred. No arrests had been made as of Monday, and the force said there was no wider threat to the public.Concertgoers described scenes of panic as the performance came to an abrupt halt and the arena lights came on. Some said people were coughing, struggling to breathe and asking for help as they made their way towards the exits.A group of friends from Scunthorpe, who were standing in the mosh pit, told the BBC they heard a “pop” before people began coughing and running. They said they were taken to the nearby Etihad Stadium for decontamination and observation.Other attendees raised concerns about security at the venue, alleging that bags had not been checked properly before entry. Co-op Live said it had a range of security measures in place, including screening systems designed to detect prohibited items.The arena said it was working closely with police to establish the cause of the incident and that the safety of visitors remained its priority.The incident has also affected Toliver’s UK tour schedule. articles.title: Thanksgiving travel forecast: Storms to batter US coasts with heavy rain and flooding
articles.summary: Two storms, including a major Nor'easter on the east coast, are expected to impact millions of people celebrating the holiday with family and friends.
articles.body:
Stormy weather on both US coasts could disrupt travel for millions over the Thanksgiving period.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicts 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.

The US National Weather Service says a series of Pacific storm systems will bring widespread rain, mountain snow, gusty winds and high surf to the West Coast this week, with coastal flood watches widely in place.

Meanwhile, Wednesday will see a storm off the south-east coast intensify and run north along the eastern seaboard. This will develop into a powerful Nor'easter storm over Thanksgiving, bringing floods, strong winds and heavy rain.

The West Coast will be badly affected in the run up to Thanksgiving, with a strong Pacific storm expected to move into the north-west on Tuesday night and affect the area throughout Wednesday.

The storm will bring particularly heavy rain because it will tap into an atmospheric river , a huge, invisible ribbon of water vapour.

Impacts will include strong winds, heavy rain at lower elevations and snow in the mountains from western Washington to Northern California.

The AAA predicts the vast majority of holiday travellers, 72.9 million, will travel by car.

Drivers could see significant delays along I-5 between Seattle and Sacramento as a result of the storm. Mountain travel could also be affected on the I-80 and I-90.

The heaviest rain is expected to miss Los Angeles and much of Southern California.

With the full Beaver moon on Tuesday , the West Coast is also expecting the highest tides of the year, coupled with the incoming storm. A coastal flood advisory is in place for the Pacific Northwest and parts of California.

The worst rain is expected to come late Wednesday into Thursday, with another storm forecast for Friday evening.

The San Francisco mayor has warned that the city is bracing for significant weather impacts in the coming days.

Daniel Lurie urged Bay Area residents to check the weather forecast before travelling and avoid unnecessary journeys.

On the East Coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding to the south-east.

It will hit Florida and the Carolinas on Wednesday, before moving northwards into the mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Thanksgiving Day.

The National Weather Service is predicting wind gusts of more than 40mph (64km/h) inland along the I-95 corridor, which connects 15 states and Washington DC.

Heavy rain is expected in New York City on Thanksgiving Day, with the city's emergency management authorities warning of "fowl weather" and a chance of coastal flooding.

The forecast has also raised questions about whether large balloons will be allowed to fly during the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Under city regulations , external , full-size balloons are not allowed if sustained wind speeds are higher than 23mph (37km/h) or gusts surpass 35mph (56km/h).

A major worry for the 5.96 million travellers who will take domestic flights for Thanksgiving is whether the weather will cause flight disruption.

Flights across the US have recently returned to normal after the national air-traffic control system recovered from a technical failure that prompted a rare national ground stop .

San Francisco and Oakland airports are under a coastal flood warning , external , with United Airlines allowing some passengers flying through San Francisco International Airport (SFO) on Wednesday to change their plans for free , external .

Both airports sit along the shoreline, which could be impacted by the exceptionally high king tides expected in the coming days. These tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño on record .

However, forecasters have lowered their estimate for Wednesday's high tide from about 3 feet above a normal high tide to 2.7 feet, which could help runways stay dry.

SFO airport authorities are still warning of potential weather impacts , external over the Thanksgiving period.

They are encouraging passengers to arrive at least two hours prior to departure for domestic flights.

articles.title: A Florida lawyer vanished from his office in 2023, leaving his keys and phone behind; three years later, the plastic surgeon convicted of killing him was sentenced to death, but his body remains missing
articles.summary: A lawyer walked into his office one morning and seemingly vanished without a trace.
articles.body: A lawyer walked into his office one morning and seemingly vanished without a trace. His phone, wallet and keys were left behind, his computer remained open, and there was no indication that he had planned to leave. Nearly three years later, the mystery surrounding his disappearance reached a grim legal conclusion, with a Florida judge sentencing the man convicted of killing him to death. Yet, despite the conviction, the lawyer’s body has never been recovered. The case of attorney Steven Cozzi and plastic surgeon Dr Tomasz Kosowski exposed a disturbing chain of events involving a bitter professional dispute, a meticulously planned killing and an unsuccessful search for human remains.Sudden disappearance raised suspicionCozzi left personal items behind when he left his Florida law office in March 2023.Her husband hadn’t heard from him and this sudden disappearance was making him worried.According to AP News, investigators later established that Cozzi had been killed inside the bathroom of his workplace, shortly after participating in a conference call connected to a prolonged legal dispute. Cozzi represented a medical practice based in Dunedin, Florida, which had been involved in an acrimonious disagreement with Kosowski. The plastic surgeon alleged that the practice had withheld thousands of dollars in billing payments and damaged his professional reputation.A calculated killing and a missing bodyProsecutors argued that Kosowski had prepared extensively before carrying out the murder. He reportedly participated in the conference call from a Toyota pickup truck parked outside the office before entering the building.Investigators said he had brought supplies including trash bags, a syringe containing a paralysing drug and a wagon to transport the body.US News reported that authorities used cellphone records and surveillance footage to trace Kosowski's movements towards a remote stretch of the Tamiami Trail, west of Miami. Investigators believe he disposed of Cozzi's body in a rubbish container that was subsequently emptied by a garbage truck. The truck driver reportedly noticed an unusually foul smell during the collection.Authorities later searched a Collier County landfill where rubbish from the route was believed to have been transported. However, the facility's routine waste-compaction process made recovering the remains virtually impossible.Evidence that sealed the prosecution's caseAlthough Cozzi's body remains missing, investigators uncovered substantial forensic evidence. His blood and DNA were discovered in the bathroom of the law office and inside the garage at Kosowski's residence.The Independent reported that investigators also found a significant collection of weapons and suspicious equipment when Kosowski was arrested. These included approximately $280,000 in cash, firearms, masks, duct tape, a ballistic vest marked EMS, law enforcement patches and a vial of succinylcholine, a paralysing drug. Court documents also indicated that around 200 guns were recovered from his home.Kosowski was convicted in September after representing himself during the trial. He presented no substantive defence, maintaining during his closing argument that prosecutors had failed to establish his guilt.Death sentence despite mitigating circumstancesOn Thursday, Pinellas Circuit Judge Joseph Bulone sentenced Kosowski to death, choosing capital punishment over life imprisonment without the possibility of release.A court-appointed special counsel said Kosowski graduated from Dartmouth College medical school and specialized in reconstructive breast surgery. The judge deemed the murder's premeditation more significant than these mitigating factors. The public defender's office has been appointed to represent Kosowski in his appeals.For Cozzi's family, the sentence marks a significant development, but not complete closure. articles.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
articles.summary: Naeem Abu Nahel, who had only been in the position for two months, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's interior ministry says.
articles.body:
An Israeli air strike has killed the head of Hamas's internal security service in Gaza.

Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said Naeem Abu Nahel was targeted by an aircraft in western Gaza City. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces .

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel had been "eliminated" by the Israeli military.

Earlier, Palestinian first responders and health officials reported that six other people had been killed in two Israeli air strikes elsewhere in Gaza on Tuesday.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, they said. The other three, including two police officers, were killed in a separate strike on a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, condemned the second attack, saying it was "part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.

The Israeli military said it had "struck terrorists in the area".

Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed by Israel and Hamas in October last year.

At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Russian governor detained in rare criminal case against regional leader
articles.summary: Andrei Chibis, head of Russia's northern Murmansk region, is the first governor to be detained for five years.
articles.body:
The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.

Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; £9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.

Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.

He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis said "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".

In a post on social media, she said her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now."

Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.

Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.

However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.

Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.

According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.

He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

articles.title: Pat Finucane was the victim of 'state-sponsored murder', inquiry hears
articles.summary: The 39-year-old solicitor was shot at his home in north Belfast by the Ulster Defence Association, in front of his wife and children, in 1989.
articles.body:
Pat Finucane was the victim of a UK "state-sponsored murder", a lawyer acting for the solicitor's family has told the public inquiry into the loyalist murder.

Danny Friedman KC told the inquiry it must answer "how far up the chain of command" the killing went.

The 39-year-old solicitor was shot at his home in north Belfast by the Ulster Defence Association (UDA) in front of his wife and children in February 1989.

Several examinations of the case have previously found evidence of state collusion.

Friedman said Finucane was killed because he was "an effective lawyer whose work had come to pose an increasing challenge to the security forces".

One of the guns used had been supplied by an agent for the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) Special Branch.

Another agent, working for the British Army, played a key role in targeting the victim.

The public inquiry opened earlier this year and is being chaired by Sir Gary Hickinbottom.

Inquiry counsel Matthew Hill has said its "core concern" is the degree to which the killers "were encouraged, assisted, protected or directed by the state ".

On Tuesday, Friedman made an opening submission on behalf of the Finucane family.

The inquiry was shown an excerpt of a 2014 BBC interview by Finucane's widow Geraldine in which said she wanted to know who instructed the gunmen.

"The gunmen didn't think this up for themselves... I wanted to know how far up the chain of command this ever went."

Echoing her words, Friedman stated: "How far up the chain of command? That is the question we submit that this inquiry exists to answer."

He said for too long the Finucane family has been met with different kinds of denial.

"The present and previous governments have admitted there was state agent involvement.

"What has never been established is who was involved in the collusion, what each of them did, and why the security forces were allowed to operate in this way."

Friedman reminded the inquiry what had previously emerged during previous examinations of the case.

An intelligence paper written in 2011 for former Prime Minister David Cameron stated the murder was the "big one" in terms of state collusion with loyalists.

Cameron had responded it was "an awful case and as bad as it gets".

Friedman pointed out a 2012 review of the murder by Sir Desmond de Silva had found no over-arching state conspiracy.

But he said that "cannot be the last word".

Another lawyer for the Finucane family, Séamus McIlroy, later described the murdered solicitor's profile in the run-up to the murder.

He said Finucane was a "fearless" solicitor who was "marked out as a target" for representing republicans.

He said loyalists had been directly incited to kill Finucane by portraying him as a member of the IRA.

"This was a complete and utter lie," McIlroy said.

He stated previous investigations and police chief constables had stated the allegation to be untrue.

"The family do not regard these lies as mere bigotry. They bore a function to attack the consequence of a highly effective lawyer," added McIlroy.

He said the family believed Finucane would be alive today if he "had not been as good at his job" and attracted "the animosity" of the police and others.

articles.title: A Las Vegas Strip parking-lot owner installed a chain-link fence and QR-code gates, restricting access for a neighbouring shopping centre's customers; Nevada's top court upheld an order to remove the obstructions
articles.summary: A dispute over customer parking on the Las Vegas Strip has ended with the state's Supreme Court backing an order on Friday to remove a fence and
articles.body: A dispute over customer parking on the Las Vegas Strip has ended with the state's Supreme Court backing an order on Friday to remove a fence and electronic gates installed around a vacant parking lot. The property owner had enclosed the land with a chain-link fence and introduced a QR-code system for motorists who wanted to park there. However, a neighbouring shopping centre said the changes interfered with access its customers were entitled to under an existing agreement. The Nevada Supreme Court upheld a lower court's order directing the owner to take down the barriers from the portion of the property covered by the agreement.According to CREdocket, a legal news website, the disagreement involves two companies that own neighbouring properties on the Las Vegas Strip. One operates a vacant parking lot, while the other owns a shopping centre housing retail outlets and restaurants. The shopping centre's owner, EC 215 Las Vegas LLC, is referred to as Silver City in the court documents. It argued that the new entry arrangements made it difficult for its customers to reach the shopping centre.The issue arose after Siegel LV North Strip Tolleson LLC bought the parking lot. The purchase came with an existing agreement that allowed Silver City and its customers to use certain parts of the land. Siegel later introduced the fence and gates, prompting the shopping centre to challenge the changes in court.New gates disrupt access to shopping centreThe parking lot was not entirely free of obligations when Siegel acquired it. An agreement known as the Parking Easement Agreement gave Silver City and its customers access to specified sections of the property.Siegel subsequently enclosed the lot with a chain-link fence. It also installed gates that required customers arriving by car to enter a QR code to park without paying.The new arrangement changed how people could move between the parking lot and the neighbouring shopping centre. Customers could no longer freely use the lot as a route to reach Silver City's property. The court order noted that the barriers affected both pedestrians and motorists.Silver City objected, saying the changes went against the access arrangement already in place. It approached the district court and asked for an order requiring Siegel to remove the fencing and gates.The company argued that the restrictions could also affect its shopping centre tenants, whose customers needed access to parking facilities.Lower court backs shopping centreThe dispute first reached the Eighth Judicial District Court in Clark County. After hearing evidence from both sides, the court sided with Silver City at the preliminary stage of the case.On July 10, 2024, it ordered Siegel to remove the barriers while the legal proceedings continued. This was a temporary measure intended to protect the shopping centre's access rights until the wider dispute could be resolved.Siegel asked the district court to reconsider its decision. The request was rejected on April 28, 2025. However, the court clarified that the company did not have to remove the entire fencing arrangement. The direction applied only to the sections covered by the parking agreement. Siegel then challenged the order before Nevada's Supreme Court.Owner argues some access was still availableSiegel's main argument was that the agreement did not prevent it from putting up barriers around its property. The company maintained that Silver City had been given access to the parking lot, but that this did not mean customers had to be allowed to enter and move through it without restrictions.In other words, Siegel argued that the QR-code gates did not necessarily violate the agreement because customers could still gain access through the system. The Supreme Court did not accept this as sufficient reason to overturn the lower court's order.The judges considered the agreement and the district court's assessment of the dispute. They found that allowing some access was not the same as complying with all the access rights available to Silver City under the agreement.The court also considered Siegel's argument that certain restrictions in the agreement applied only when construction of a parking garage began. It found that this did not establish that the company was free to block or restrict access before construction started.The Supreme Court did not make a final ruling on every disagreement over the meaning of the agreement. It examined whether the lower court had reasonable grounds to believe Silver City could succeed in its case and needed protection while the proceedings continued. It found no sufficient reason to interfere with that decision.Shopping centre warns of impact on tenantsSiegel also questioned why the shopping centre needed a court order when any financial losses could potentially be recovered through compensation.Silver City argued that the consequences of restricted parking could go beyond lost business or reduced revenue. Its agreements with shopping centre tenants included responsibilities relating to parking access for their customers.If the barriers remained, the shopping centre could face difficulties meeting those commitments. This could affect its business relationships with the retailers and restaurants operating on the property.The Supreme Court considered this a significant concern. It agreed that the potential damage was not limited to losses that could easily be calculated and repaid later.The judges therefore found that the district court had sufficient evidence to conclude that financial compensation alone might not address the problem.Siegel also suggested that the gates could have been modified instead of being removed. The company argued that changes to the system might have allowed customers to reach the shopping centre while keeping some restrictions around the parking lot.However, it did not point to any particular alternative that the lower court had failed to consider. Silver City had sought the removal of the barriers, and the district court had granted that request for the areas covered by the agreement.The Supreme Court said its decision did not prevent the parties from discussing a modified arrangement during the continuing legal proceedings.Court rejects owner's safety concernsSiegel further argued that removing the fence and gates could create problems for the parking lot, including concerns involving crime and homelessness.The company wanted these risks to be considered while deciding whether the barriers should remain in place.However, the Supreme Court pointed out that Siegel had known about these concerns when it purchased the property. It said the company could not use problems that already existed at the time of purchase as a reason to justify installing the barriers later. After examining the arguments, the court found no grounds to overturn the district court's order.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
